Current status of -omics research in platyhelminth parasites of teleost fish

Abstract

Parasitic platyhelminths (Trematoda, Monogenea, and Cestoda) are responsible for widespread disease in wild and cultured fish in both freshwater and marine environments globally, impacting both human health and the sustainability of aquaculture industries. Research into these parasites primarily aims to understand the impact of infections on host species, as well as developing management strategies to reduce or eliminate disease. -Omics-based research can assist in uncovering the biology of these parasites across a range of key areas, including understanding host-pathogen interactions, identifying novel drug and vaccine targets, and recognizing the overall diversity of parasite species. To date, the application of -omics technologies to piscivorous platyhelminths has been limited. This Chapter focuses on the current availability of -omics research in fish platyhelminths, with a primary focus on parasites with definitive fish hosts, and argues that the application of these technologies may provide unprecedented opportunities for the development of novel sustainable strategies for infection and disease management and control.

Introduction

Fish serve as an important food source globally, with whole populations relying on fish as a primary source of protein. As such, understanding the parasites associated with fish is vital. Parasitic flatworms (Phylum Platyhelminthes), consisting of Trematodes, Monogeneans, and Cestodes, are common in both freshwater and marine fish worldwide, causing significant health issues to their hosts. The life cycles of these parasites can be complex. For instance, in the case of digenean trematodes and cestodes, life cycles can involve multiple hosts, where fish can act as either a definitive or an intermediate host. Multiple intermediate hosts, or vectors, can be utilized by these parasites, making understanding their biology exceptionally complex. In contrast, monogeneans are characterized by a direct life cycle, requiring only the fish as their host. While direct life cycles mostly impact fish, parasites with more complex life cycles often impact livestock and human health. The incidence of parasitic flatworms in marine and freshwater fish globally is considerable and summarized in Table 1.
One area in which parasitic platyhelminths exert a large economic impact is represented by the farmed fish industry. Increased demand for fish as a high protein food source has resulted in the rapid expansion of aquaculture of a variety of fish species globally. In 2022, global aquaculture production reached 130.9 million tonnes, comprising 59 percent of total aquaculture and fisheries production (FAO, 2022). However, aspects of fish farming including high stocking densities of fish, and open water culture, which increases the likelihood of interactions between fish and vectors of parasites, may result in significant increases in the incidence and severity of parasitic outbreaks in fish (Ogawa, 2015). Hence, losses from mortalities, reduced growth, and stress of fish, as well as associated treatment costs, may have significant economic impacts on industries. Amongst the most impactful parasitic flatworms affecting aquaculture are digenean trematodes, with blood flukes causing significant pathology across a range of species (Power et al., 2020). Inherent difficulties in managing some parasitic infections may further exacerbate their impact. For example, infections by the monogenean Benedenia seriolae are particularly difficult to control in aquaculture environments, as the eggs of this parasite are filamentous and can become tangled within the surrounding nets, thus resulting in reinfections post treatment (Ogawa, 2015). Flatworms with definitive fish hosts often cause more significant pathology, compared to parasites that infect fish as metacercaria, although species such as Galactoscomum nagasakiense, which causes diseases with similar signs to whirling disease, are notable exceptions (Kamegai and Ogawa, 2024). The complex life cycles of some parasite species make their management difficult, as interactions with multiple hosts need to be considered. Limited knowledge of life cycles is a major roadblock in the management of these parasites.
The impact of food borne illnesses from parasitic platyhelminths to human health is substantial. Consequently, much of the research into parasites with fish hosts has focused on these zoonotic species. Proximity of intermediate hosts to human populations can result in transmission and subsequent disease in people (Keiser and Utzinger, 2009; Sithithaworn et al., 2023). Both Trematoda and Cestoda include zoonotic species that infect humans via fish consumption and that can cause significant pathology (Furst et al., 2012). Two of the major fish-borne diseases, opisthorchiasis and clonorchiasis, are caused by the liver flukes Opisthorchis viverrini and Clonorchis sinensis respectively; the infection, which is estimated to impact up to 40 million individuals annually, is acquired following ingestion of raw or undercooked fish containing the parasites (Sithithaworn et al., 2023). Whilst cestodes are also significant pathogens, resulting illnesses are generally less severe than those caused by trematodes. The genus Diphyllobothrium includes most of the fish-borne cestodes, with Dibothriocephalus latus (fish tapeworm) being the most reported (Bardhan, 2022). Notwithstanding the impact of zoonotic platyhelminths on the burden of neglected tropical diseases worldwide, extensively reviewed elsewhere (de Sousa et al., 2013; Haçariz and Sayers, 2016; International Helminth Genomes Consortium Genomes, 2019; Bennett and Robinson, 2021; Callejas-Hernández et al., 2023), this Chapter focuses largely on non-zoonotic platyhelminth parasites, primarily those which use teleost fish as their definitive hosts.
The term “-omics,” refers to the study and analysis of biological molecules on a large scale, to understand the structure or function of whole biological systems. This area of research focuses primarily on the study of genes, transcripts, proteins, and metabolites (genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics, respectively), as well as their modifications (for example epigenomics, i.e. the study of modifications to the DNA and chromatin; or epitranscriptomics, i.e. the study of modifications affecting RNA function), and interactions. -Omics studies of parasites have significantly expanded over the last few decades, with the development of high-throughput technologies making these areas of research faster and more efficient, as well as more affordable. The progression of nucleic acid sequencing technologies from next-generation to third-generation sequencing and chromosome conformation capture sequencing (Hi-C) has made the assembly of high-quality genomes and transcriptomes of parasites more accessible than ever (Mitreva, 2022). Additionally, the expansion of bioinformatics tools has been instrumental in the progression of -omics research. Computational tools for the analysis of large-scale datasets have improved the speed at which -omics data can be processed, and advances in supercomputing have allowed for the development of large, interactive and user-friendly -omics databases (Rudakiya et al., 2024).
The gap in knowledge surrounding the fundamental and molecular biology of many parasites is one of the largest challenges that hinders the development of effective control strategies. Indeed, the process of identifying genes that may represent viable targets for drug and vaccine development, as well as developing and testing the efficacy of novel vaccines and treatments, is long and costly. In particular, the discovery of new anthelmintics has been slow, with only three new drug classes discovered in the last two decades (Nixon et al., 2020). Whilst workflows involving multiple -omics methods have been successful in accelerating the process of potential drug development (by screening hundreds of targets simultaneously; Schmidt et al., 2022), -omics studies of platyhelminths with definitive fish hosts are still scant.

Section snippets

Molecular studies of piscivorous platyhelminths

Prior to the advancement of -omics technologies, sequence data for many parasites were limited to partial gene sequences, with only model species (e.g. Schistosoma mansoni, S. japonicum, Echinococcus multilocularis, E. granulosus) being analyzed at a genomic level. Molecular studies of fish platyhelminths have traditionally focused on specific markers developed for taxonomic investigations, rather than on the generation of whole genome sequences. Conclusions and future research

To date, the depth and breadth of -omics research in piscivorous platyhelminths has been limited. Despite the economic impact of platyhelminths in aquaculture, large-scale genomic sequences are available for only eight species of platyhelminths with definitive fish hosts, with most of these genomes available in “draft” form. Functional -omics resources are even rarer. A single glycomic profile is available for one trematode species, and no transcriptomics, proteomics, or secretomics studies
